article_blocks.text: Strain Type: 80% Indica / 20% Sativa
Genetics: Undisclosed Canadian purple genetics
Breeder: Great White North Seed Co.
THC Content: 22%
CBD Content: N/A
Terpene Profile: myrcene , caryophyllene , linalool
Primary Flavors: Sweet fruit, perfume, floral notes, herbs
Flowering Time (Indoor): 8 weeks
Outdoor Harvest Time: mid-September
Indoor Yield: Moderate
Outdoor Yield: ¼–¾ lb per plant
Grow Difficulty: Easy to moderate

Lethal Purple belongs to a distinctive chapter of Canadian cannabis history in which breeders were trying to produce marijuana capable of finishing outdoors before northern autumn weather destroyed the crop. Long before purple weed became associated primarily with California dessert weed strains , Great White North Seed Co. was offering a tall, early-finishing purple hybrid bred for outdoor gardens in Manitoba and other short-season regions. The original catalog described Lethal Purple as a productive indica-sativa cross with a large Christmas-tree structure, perfume-like aroma, sweet fruity flavor, roughly eight weeks of flowering, and a mid-September harvest.

Great White North specifically promoted its outdoor varieties as proven performers that had been cultivated for years under Manitoba conditions. Later Canadian versions became especially associated with dark purple flowers and a heavier indica character, but the strain’s central identity remained the same: early maturity, strong coloration, substantial production, and deeply aromatic buds. For growers interested in old Canadian weed genetics, Lethal Purple is significant not because of a fashionable pedigree but because it represents practical northern breeding from an era when surviving September frost could matter more than reaching an extreme THC percentage.
Genetics and Lineage

One of the most important facts about Lethal Purple is that its precise parentage was never clearly disclosed by Great White North Seed Co. The surviving original catalog simply calls it an “indica/sativa cross,” without naming individual parents. This makes several pedigrees circulated today difficult to support. Claims involving Blueberry and Haze , Killer Queen and Mendocino Purps , or other specific varieties should not be presented as established genetics for the original strain unless better breeder documentation emerges. The safest lineage description is therefore an old Canadian indica-sativa hybrid selected by Great White North for early outdoor performance.

Later preservation work offers additional clues without completely resolving the ancestry. Anthos Seeds produced a preservation run reportedly derived from Great White North stock dating to approximately 1991, describing its preserved Lethal Purple as an inbred “Indica × Purple Indica” population obtained from Canadian growers who had maintained it for commercial production. Those plants were noted for deep purple buds, heavy yields, stability, and old-school incense character. Because that preservation description differs somewhat from Great White North’s earlier indica-sativa classification and harvest timing, it is best understood as evidence of the strain’s long Canadian history rather than proof of an exact original pedigree. Decades of preservation, selection, and reproduction can alter how a population behaves while retaining its recognizable core traits.
Effects and Experience

The classic Lethal Purple experience leans toward physical relaxation without necessarily eliminating mental function. Later Canadian descriptions classify the strain as approximately 80% indica and emphasize a strong stone, while historical accounts consistently portray it as powerful rather than mild. The initial stage can bring a pronounced shift in mood and sensory perception, followed by an increasingly comfortable heaviness through the body. Despite that relaxing foundation, a trace of sativa influence can preserve enough mental activity for music, conversation, television, or other low-pressure recreation.

What distinguishes the strain from especially narcotic pure indicas is that the head may remain relatively clear while the body relaxes. Moderate consumption can feel peaceful and pleasantly detached rather than immediately sleep-inducing. With a larger dose, however, the physical portion becomes much stronger and the experience may move toward lethargy, reduced motivation, and eventual drowsiness. For this reason, Lethal Purple generally makes more sense during late afternoon or evening than before work requiring fast reactions or sustained concentration.

Reliable cannabinoid testing from the original plants does not survive, so modern claims assigning a precise THC percentage to the cultivar should be approached cautiously. Flower sold under the name today may come from preserved seed populations, recreations, or unrelated modern interpretations. Actual potency can therefore vary considerably. Consumers should rely on batch-specific laboratory results when available rather than assuming that historical reputation translates into a universal THC concentration.
Medical Benefits

The predominantly relaxing profile may interest medical cannabis consumers who prefer weed with substantial body effects. THC-rich cultivars of this general character are sometimes used in the evening when temporary stress, muscular tension, appetite difficulties, or physical discomfort make relaxation difficult. A calmer mental state combined with heavier bodily effects may also make the later portion of the experience useful to consumers who choose marijuana before bedtime.

There is no clinical research establishing Lethal Purple itself as a treatment for pain, insomnia, anxiety, depression, or another medical condition. That limitation is especially important with an older cultivar whose chemistry has never been standardized. Different surviving versions may contain substantially different cannabinoid and terpene profiles. High-THC cannabis can also cause dizziness, anxiety, dry mouth, impaired coordination, or excessive sedation. Medical consumers should base decisions on the laboratory-tested product they actually possess and seek appropriate medical guidance when cannabis is being used for ongoing symptoms.
Flavor Profile and Aroma

Perfume is one of the oldest documented descriptors for Lethal Purple. Great White North’s period catalog specifically characterized the aroma as perfumy and the flavor as sweet and fruity. That profile places the strain closer to traditional floral purple cannabis than to modern grape-candy hybrids. Mature flowers can suggest sweet berries or dark fruit, but floral perfume, herbs, and unmistakable cannabis pungency give the bouquet greater depth.

Preserved versions have added another dimension to that description. The Anthos preservation line is associated with incense, herbs, and sweetness, suggesting that some of the older population carries a dry, resinous, almost temple-incense quality beneath the fruit. These darker tones can become more obvious after curing, when the initially green and floral aroma settles into something richer and more rounded.

No authoritative terpene analysis survives from the original Great White North stock. Linalool could reasonably contribute floral or perfume-like qualities, myrcene may support fruit and herbal depth, and caryophyllene could account for spice, but such associations should not be confused with confirmed laboratory measurements. Phenotype, climate, harvest timing, and curing technique can all significantly change how Lethal Purple smells and tastes.
Growing Information

Lethal Purple was fundamentally an outdoor strain. Great White North Seed Co. described its catalog as containing hardy outdoor varieties proven under Manitoba conditions, and Lethal Purple was listed specifically for outdoor growing. The original plant developed a large Christmas-tree shape and reached roughly six to seven feet, considerably taller than the squat appearance that its later indica-heavy reputation might suggest. Flowering lasted approximately eight weeks, with outdoor harvest around the middle of September. For northern growers, that early maturity was a major advantage because it allowed the flowers to finish before prolonged cold, rain, or frost became dominant.

Original yields were given at approximately one-quarter to three-quarters of a pound per plant. Later Canadian Bred material described six-foot plants capable of approaching one pound under favorable conditions, while also emphasizing the cultivar’s intensely purple appearance. Such figures should be treated as potential rather than guaranteed output. Direct sunlight, root volume, plant spacing, fertility, summer temperatures, and the length of vegetative growth can dramatically alter outdoor production.

Branching is naturally useful for distributing flowers across the plant. Early topping or gentle training can broaden the canopy further, although unrestricted outdoor specimens already tend toward a wide Christmas-tree architecture. Because the cultivar was selected under Canadian conditions, it is particularly interesting for growers in locations where long-flowering tropical genetics are impractical. Plants should still be inspected for mold as autumn approaches, especially when purple flowers become dense and nighttime humidity increases.

Color is another major cultivation attraction. Many purple strains require low temperatures before anthocyanin pigments become dramatic, but preserved and later-described Lethal Purple populations have been noted for exceptionally strong genetic coloration. Mature buds may range from violet to extremely dark purple rather than merely showing purple tips. Growers should still maintain healthy temperatures instead of intentionally subjecting plants to damaging cold simply to increase pigmentation.
FAQ
What are the genetics of Lethal Purple?

The exact parents of the original Lethal Purple have never been reliably disclosed. Great White North Seed Co.’s historical catalog described it simply as an indica-sativa cross developed for early outdoor production in Canada. Later preservation stock has been described as an indica × purple indica population, but that does not establish the exact original parents.
Who bred Lethal Purple?

The original strain is associated with Great White North Seed Co. in Canada. Historical catalogs from the Canadian seed trade list Lethal Purple among the company’s Manitoba-proven outdoor cultivars. The genetics were later maintained and distributed by other Canadian sources and preservation breeders.
Is Lethal Purple indica or sativa?

It is an indica-sativa hybrid that later releases have frequently described as about 80% indica. Its body-heavy stone supports that classification, although the original plant’s six-to-seven-foot outdoor structure and breeder description indicate meaningful hybrid influence.
When does Lethal Purple finish outdoors?

The original Great White North listing placed harvest around mid-September after approximately eight weeks of flowering. Some later preservation lines finish later, which is why the provenance of the seed stock matters when planning an outdoor harvest.
What does Lethal Purple taste like?

Sweet fruit and perfume are the most historically documented traits. Floral notes, herbs, berries, spice, and incense may also appear depending on the particular population and phenotype. Preserved old Canadian stock has been specifically associated with sweet, herbal, incense-like smoke.
Final Thoughts on Lethal Purple

Lethal Purple deserves recognition as an old Canadian outdoor cultivar rather than another modern purple strain with an uncertain marketing pedigree. Great White North Seed Co. developed and distributed it during a period when Canadian breeders needed weed that could produce meaningful yields and mature before severe northern autumn weather arrived. A mid-September harvest, roughly eight-week bloom, six-to-seven-foot structure, sweet perfumed flowers, and substantial outdoor productivity made it well suited to that purpose.

Its incomplete pedigree should be treated as part of the historical record rather than filled in with unsupported parent names. What survives is more informative than speculation: Lethal Purple is a hardy Canadian hybrid with strong purple expression, fruit-and-floral aromatics, relaxing effects, and a long reputation for outdoor performance. Preservation efforts based on decades-old Great White North material further demonstrate that the genetics were important enough for growers to maintain long after the original seed market changed. For enthusiasts interested in early-finishing marijuana, Canadian breeding history, or purple cannabis that predates today’s dessert era, Lethal Purple remains a particularly distinctive old-school cultivar.
